subtopic_detail: Both feet turning inwards when running in a four year old who sits between his heels with a normal neurological examination
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a four year old boy whose parents are worried that both feet turn inwards when he runs and that he trips more than other children at kindergarten. They have been told by a relative that he needs special boots.

He walked at thirteen months, has no pain, and keeps up with his friends at the playground. His parents say he always sits on the floor between his heels with his knees together.

data_table.Examination: Both patellae point inwards on walking, hip internal rotation 80 degrees with external rotation 15 degrees bilaterally in the prone position, thigh foot angle neutral on both sides, lateral borders of both feet straight with no forefoot deviation, tone power and reflexes normal in both legs with downgoing plantar responses, symmetrical leg lengths, no joint swelling

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer him to an orthopaedic surgeon to be assessed for a derotation osteotomy of both femurs before he starts school next year
options.rationale: Femoral derotation osteotomy is a major procedure reserved for severe rotational deformity that persists beyond about eight to ten years with genuine functional or cosmetic disability. Offering it to a four year old with a condition that resolves on its own in the great majority is disproportionate. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

options.text: Reassure the parents that this is physiological femoral anteversion and review only if it persists beyond the age of eight
options.rationale: Increased hip internal rotation with correspondingly reduced external rotation, a neutral thigh foot angle and straight lateral foot borders localises the rotation to the femur, and femoral anteversion peaks around four to six years and then remodels spontaneously in almost all children. Habitual W sitting is a consequence of the anteversion rather than its cause. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

options.text: Prescribe a night time derotation brace to be worn until the rotational profile of both of his legs has normalised
options.rationale: Braces, corrective shoes and twister cables have all been shown not to alter the natural history of rotational variants and they disturb sleep and self image for no benefit. Bracing retains a role in structural conditions such as developmental dysplasia of the hip and idiopathic scoliosis. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

options.text: Refer him for serial casting of both feet to correct the inward deviation of the forefoot that is causing his gait
options.rationale: Serial casting treats metatarsus adductus, in which the lateral border of the foot is curved and the forefoot deviates medially, and his feet have straight lateral borders. The level of the rotation is determined by examining the hip, the thigh foot angle and the foot separately. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and spine to look for a neurological cause of his in-toeing and his tripping
options.rationale: Spastic diplegia is the important neurological mimic of in-toeing, but it produces increased tone, brisk reflexes, upgoing plantar responses and usually a history of delayed walking, none of which are present. Imaging is warranted when the rotational deformity is asymmetrical or when the neurological examination is abnormal. (Source: RCH CPG: In-toeing)

explanation.summary: In-toeing is one of the commonest reasons for orthopaedic referral in early childhood and is almost always one of three physiological rotational variants, each of which has a characteristic age of presentation and a specific examination finding that localises it. Metatarsus adductus presents in infancy with a curved lateral foot border, internal tibial torsion presents in the toddler years with an internally rotated thigh foot angle, and femoral anteversion presents between about three and six years with markedly increased hip internal rotation and reduced external rotation. The rotational profile examination, performed with the child prone, separates these in a few minutes without any imaging. All three remodel spontaneously with growth, and no orthosis, shoe modification or exercise programme has been shown to change the outcome, so the intervention is explanation and reassurance with a defined review point. The findings that should prompt further assessment are asymmetry, pain, an abnormal neurological examination, or persistence with functional disability into later childhood.
key_points: The rotational profile examination localises in-toeing to the foot, the tibia or the femur.
Increased internal with reduced external hip rotation indicates femoral anteversion.
A curved lateral foot border indicates metatarsus adductus rather than a rotational problem above it.
Braces, corrective shoes and exercises do not alter the natural history of any of these variants.
Asymmetry, pain or abnormal tone and reflexes are the findings that justify further assessment.
explanation.pearls: Measure hip rotation with the child prone and the knees flexed to 90 degrees, because total hip rotation stays roughly constant at around 90 to 100 degrees throughout childhood and it is the shift of that arc towards internal rotation, rather than the absolute internal rotation figure, that identifies femoral anteversion.

sources.label: Australian Orthopaedic Association: Paediatric lower limb variants
BMJ Best Practice: Gait abnormalities in children

subtopic_detail: Three weeks of pale greasy stools and weight loss in a preschooler after a childcare outbreak of loose motions
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in a general clinic seeing a three year old girl whose mother reports three weeks of loose, pale, foul smelling motions that float, with a lot of wind and a swollen tummy. She has lost 0.8 kg over that time.

Four other children at her childcare centre have had similar prolonged loose motions in the past month. There has been no blood in the stool, no fever and no vomiting. She has eaten bread and cereal daily since she was seven months old without any previous bowel trouble, and her growth had tracked the 50th centile until this illness.

data_table.Examination: Mildly distended soft abdomen, no organomegaly, no mouth ulcers, no perianal disease, no rash, no clubbing, mucous membranes moist
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count within normal limits, C-reactive protein less than 5 mg/L (less than 5), albumin 38 g/L (35 to 50)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Send a faecal specimen for protozoal nucleic acid amplification testing before starting any antimicrobial treatment
options.rationale: Prolonged non bloody steatorrhoea with flatulence, bloating and weight loss following a childcare cluster is the classic picture of giardiasis, and faecal nucleic acid amplification testing is far more sensitive than a single microscopy specimen. Confirming the organism before treating avoids committing a child to nitroimidazole therapy for what may prove to be a different diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Start oral metronidazole empirically for three days and review her symptoms and weight in the clinic in two weeks
options.rationale: Empirical treatment is reasonable only when testing is unavailable, and here it would remove the chance to confirm an organism that must be notified and traced back to the childcare centre. Treatment is correct once the diagnosis is established, and single dose tinidazole is the preferred Australian regimen in children who can take it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

options.text: Request coeliac serology with a total immunoglobulin A level and arrange gastroenterology review for possible biopsy
options.rationale: Coeliac disease produces exactly this stool description and weight loss, but it does not arrive abruptly three weeks ago in a child who has eaten gluten uneventfully for over two years, nor does it cluster among four other children at the same centre. It becomes the priority if the stool testing is negative and symptoms persist. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children

options.text: Advise a two week trial of a strictly lactose free diet and review whether the stool frequency and bloating improve
options.rationale: Secondary lactose intolerance does follow gastroenteritis and can cause bloating and loose stools, but it does not cause progressive weight loss over three weeks and it does not explain the fatty floating stools. A dietary trial here delays a diagnosis that requires specific treatment and public health follow up. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children

options.text: Arrange an abdominal ultrasound to look for a structural cause of her distension and her three weeks of loose stools
options.rationale: Imaging has no role in a well child with a soft abdomen, no organomegaly and normal inflammatory markers, and a normal scan would falsely reassure everyone. Ultrasound earns its place when there is an abdominal mass, organomegaly or a suspicion of intussusception. (Source: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children)
source_refs: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children

explanation.summary: Giardia duodenalis is the commonest protozoal cause of persistent diarrhoea in Australian children and spreads readily by the faecal oral route in childcare centres, where asymptomatic carriage sustains outbreaks. The organism blunts the small bowel villi and causes fat malabsorption, which is why the stools are pale, greasy and offensive rather than watery, and why weight loss appears within weeks. Faecal nucleic acid amplification testing has largely replaced the three specimen microscopy request because cyst shedding is intermittent and a single microscopy sample misses around half of cases. Treatment in Australia is a nitroimidazole, with tinidazole as a single dose being the usual first choice in children old enough to swallow it, and household contacts are treated only if symptomatic. Giardiasis is notifiable in most jurisdictions, which matters here because identifying the organism triggers exclusion and hygiene measures at the centre.
key_points: Pale greasy floating stools with flatulence and weight loss point to small bowel malabsorption, not colitis.
A childcare cluster with prolonged non bloody diarrhoea strongly suggests giardiasis.
Faecal nucleic acid amplification testing outperforms single specimen microscopy because cyst shedding is intermittent.
Long standing uneventful gluten exposure with abrupt onset argues against coeliac disease as the cause.
Confirming the organism triggers public health exclusion measures at the childcare centre.
explanation.pearls: Children with giardiasis should be excluded from childcare until they have had no loose stool for 24 hours, and a single 50 mg per kg dose of tinidazole to a maximum of 2 g cures around 90 per cent, which is why persistent symptoms after treatment should prompt a test for post infectious lactose intolerance rather than a second course.

sources.label: Royal Children's Hospital Melbourne: Chronic diarrhoea in children

subtopic_detail: Screaming and thrashing an hour and a half after falling asleep in a preschooler who has no memory of it next day
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar seeing a four year old girl whose parents describe frightening episodes three or four nights a week. About ninety minutes after she falls asleep she sits up screaming, pushes them away and thrashes about with her eyes wide open, appearing terrified and not recognising them.

Each episode lasts around five minutes and she then settles back to sleep. In the morning she is cheerful and remembers nothing about it. Her father had similar episodes as a boy. She does not snore and has no daytime sleepiness.

data_table.Examination: Growth along the 50th centile, development age appropriate with fluent sentences, tonsils not enlarged on inspection, no dysmorphic features, neurological examination normal with normal tone power and reflexes, no skin stigmata of a neurocutaneous syndrome

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure her parents, advise safety measures in the bedroom and explain that the episodes settle without treatment
options.rationale: Arousal from the deepest non rapid eye movement sleep in the first third of the night, with unresponsiveness during the event and complete amnesia afterwards in a child with a family history, is a night terror, and these resolve spontaneously through childhood. Parents are advised not to wake or restrain the child and to make the bedroom and stairs safe. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children

options.text: Arrange an overnight sleep electroencephalogram to look for frontal lobe seizures arising out of sleep
options.rationale: Sleep related hypermotor seizures are the key mimic but are stereotyped, brief, often occur several times in one night and typically leave the child aware or rousable afterwards. An electroencephalogram is warranted for stereotyped repetitive events, daytime episodes or any developmental regression. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children

options.text: Commence low dose clonazepam at bedtime and review the frequency of the episodes in the clinic after four weeks
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines suppress deep non rapid eye movement sleep and are occasionally used for parasomnias, but they are not justified for a benign self limiting condition in a preschooler. They are reserved for episodes that are dangerous or that persist and disrupt the family severely despite all behavioural measures. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Psychotropic)

options.text: Refer her for polysomnography and adenotonsillectomy assessment on the basis that sleep disordered breathing is triggering the episodes
options.rationale: Obstructive sleep apnoea does fragment sleep and can provoke parasomnias, which is why it is asked about, but she does not snore, has no daytime sleepiness and has normal sized tonsils. A sleep study is indicated when snoring, witnessed apnoea or daytime symptoms are present alongside the parasomnia. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children

options.text: Refer her to a child psychologist on the basis that these episodes represent anxiety dreams requiring trauma focused assessment
options.rationale: Nightmares occur in the second half of the night during rapid eye movement sleep, the child wakes fully, is consolable and recalls the dream, all of which are the opposite of what is described here. Psychological assessment is appropriate for recurrent distressing nightmares, particularly after a traumatic event. (Source: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children

explanation.summary: Night terrors are a disorder of arousal from slow wave sleep and affect a substantial minority of preschool and early primary school children, with a strong familial tendency. They are separated from nightmares by four features: timing in the first third of the night rather than the second half, profound unresponsiveness and inconsolability during the event rather than a child who wakes and seeks comfort, marked autonomic arousal with sweating, tachycardia and dilated pupils, and complete amnesia the next morning. The important differential is sleep related hypermotor epilepsy, suggested by highly stereotyped brief events, clustering several times in a single night, or a persisting abnormality on waking. Sleep deprivation, irregular bedtimes, fever and untreated obstructive sleep apnoea all increase the frequency of arousal parasomnias, so addressing those is the practical intervention along with safety proofing the sleeping environment. Parents should be told explicitly not to wake or restrain the child, since doing so prolongs and intensifies the episode.
key_points: Night terrors arise from slow wave sleep in the first third of the night with complete amnesia afterwards.
Nightmares occur later in the night, the child wakes fully, is consolable and remembers the dream.
Stereotyped brief events clustering several times a night suggest sleep related seizures.
Sleep deprivation, irregular bedtimes, fever and sleep disordered breathing increase frequency.
Parents should not wake or restrain the child, and the sleeping environment is made safe.
explanation.pearls: Scheduled awakenings, in which the parent rouses the child briefly about fifteen to thirty minutes before the usual time of the event for a week or two, reduce night terror frequency substantially and are worth offering to exhausted families before any medication is considered.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Sleep problems in children

subtopic_detail: Flattening at the back of the head in a five month old with the ear on the flattened side sitting forward of the other
stem:
You are the general practice registrar seeing a five month old girl whose parents are distressed about the shape of her head. They say the back right side looks squashed and that it has become more obvious over the past two months, and they have read that a helmet may be needed.

She was born at term, rolls both ways, has good head control and has no feeding difficulty. She sleeps on her back and spends much of the day in a rocker.

data_table.Examination: Flattening of the right occiput with the right ear displaced anteriorly relative to the left and mild fullness of the right forehead, giving a parallelogram outline when viewed from above, no ridging palpable over any suture, no mastoid bulge behind either ear, anterior fontanelle soft and open, head circumference tracking the 50th centile, full passive neck rotation to both sides

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Advise counter positioning with supervised tummy time and cot repositioning, and review her head shape in two months
options.rationale: An anteriorly displaced ear with ipsilateral forehead fullness produces the parallelogram of deformational plagiocephaly, which responds to repositioning because the skull is still growing rapidly at five months. Most cases improve substantially with conservative measures and need nothing further. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Refer her urgently to the craniofacial service on the basis that a fused lambdoid suture is the likeliest explanation
options.rationale: Lambdoid synostosis is the near pair that must be excluded, but it pushes the ear on the affected side posteriorly and produces a mastoid bulge with a trapezoid rather than parallelogram outline, and neither feature is present. The direction the ear is displaced is the single most useful bedside discriminator. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Arrange a computed tomography scan of the skull with three dimensional reconstruction to assess all of the cranial sutures
options.rationale: Computed tomography delivers a substantial radiation dose to a developing brain and is not needed when the clinical pattern is diagnostic of a positional deformity. It is reserved for cases where synostosis is genuinely suspected on examination and a craniofacial team requests it. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Refer her now for a moulding helmet orthosis to be fitted, because the deformity has been progressing over recent months
options.rationale: Helmet therapy is expensive, demanding for families and has not been shown in randomised comparison to outperform repositioning for mild to moderate deformity. It is considered only for severe deformity that has failed an adequate trial of repositioning, usually between five and eight months of age. (Source: RCH CPG: Plagiocephaly)

options.text: Refer her to physiotherapy for treatment of an underlying tightness of the neck muscles driving the positional preference
options.rationale: Torticollis commonly drives plagiocephaly and physiotherapy is then essential, but this infant has full passive rotation in both directions and no palpable muscle mass, so there is no restriction to treat. The presence or absence of a passive rotation deficit decides whether physiotherapy is required. (Source: RCH CPG: Torticollis)

explanation.summary: Deformational plagiocephaly became common after supine sleeping was correctly promoted to reduce sudden unexpected death in infancy, and it reflects external moulding of a soft skull rather than any abnormality of the sutures. Viewed from above the head forms a parallelogram, because the occipital flattening pushes the ipsilateral ear and forehead forward, whereas true lambdoid synostosis restricts growth and pulls the ipsilateral ear backwards with a compensatory mastoid bulge, giving a trapezoid. That single distinction spares almost every infant a computed tomography scan. Conservative management works because the skull grows fastest in the first year, so the earlier repositioning begins the more correction is achieved. Parents need explicit reassurance that the condition does not affect brain growth or development, since much of their distress comes from fearing that it does.
key_points: Parallelogram head shape with the ear displaced forward indicates a positional deformity.
Trapezoid shape with the ear displaced backwards and a mastoid bulge suggests lambdoid synostosis.
Palpable sutural ridging and a falling or rising head circumference are red flags for synostosis.
Repositioning and tummy time are first line and most effective before six months of age.
Always check passive neck rotation, since coexisting torticollis requires physiotherapy.
explanation.pearls: Assess the head from directly above the vertex rather than from the front, because the anterior or posterior position of the ear relative to its fellow is the finding that separates deformational plagiocephaly from lambdoid synostosis and it is almost invisible from any other angle.

subtopic_detail: Blotchy pink rash appearing on the trunk of a well eleven month old on the day a three day high fever settled
stem:
You are the doctor on an after hours general practice shift seeing an eleven month old boy whose mother brings him because a rash appeared this morning. He had a temperature up to 39.5 degrees Celsius for the previous three days, during which he was irritable but kept feeding, and the fever broke overnight.

She says the rash is pink and blotchy over his chest and tummy and has spread up onto his neck, and that it goes pale if she presses a glass against it. He is now playing on the floor of the consulting room. His immunisations are up to date and he has had no antibiotics.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 118 beats per minute, blood pressure 92/56 mmHg, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute, SpO2 99 per cent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius
data_table.Examination: Blanching pink macular and maculopapular rash over the trunk and neck sparing the face and limbs, no conjunctival injection, no coryza, moist lips with no mucosal change, no cervical lymphadenopathy, no desquamation of the hands or feet, no hepatosplenomegaly, no bruising or petechiae

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Explain the illness as a self limiting viral exanthem, give written advice on when to return, and arrange no investigations
options.rationale: A high fever for three days that defervesces as a blanching truncal rash appears in a well infant is the defining sequence of roseola infantum, caused by human herpesvirus 6. The diagnosis is clinical, the illness is self limiting and testing changes nothing. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Notify the public health unit of a probable measles case and send a throat swab and serology for measles confirmation
options.rationale: Measles is the notifiable mimic worth considering in any febrile child with a rash, but its rash appears while the fever is still high and is preceded by cough, coryza and conjunctivitis, none of which are present here. The temporal relationship of rash to fever is the discriminator between the two. (Source: Communicable Diseases Network Australia: Measles)

options.text: Admit him for intravenous antibiotics after taking blood cultures, given the recent height and duration of his documented fever
options.rationale: A child who is playing, afebrile and has a blanching rash without petechiae has no features of invasive bacterial infection, and admission would expose him to unnecessary cannulation and antibiotics. Non blanching lesions, toxicity or an ill appearance would change this decision immediately. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Request a full blood count and blood film today to exclude an underlying haematological malignancy presenting with fever and rash
options.rationale: Leukaemia can present with fever and skin lesions, but those lesions are petechiae or bruises rather than a blanching exanthem, and it is accompanied by pallor, lymphadenopathy or organomegaly, all absent here. Bleeding into the skin rather than a blanching rash is what should trigger a film. (Source: RCH CPG: Febrile child)

options.text: Commence oral amoxicillin for a presumed bacterial cause of his three day fever and review the rash again in forty eight hours
options.rationale: There is no bacterial focus and the illness has already resolved spontaneously, so antibiotics offer only adverse effects and resistance. Amoxicillin given to a child with undiagnosed infectious mononucleosis also provokes a florid rash that muddies the picture further. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Antibiotic)

explanation.summary: Roseola infantum, also called exanthem subitum or sixth disease, is caused predominantly by human herpesvirus 6 and affects children between about six months and two years. Its signature is three to five days of high fever in a child who remains reasonably well, followed by abrupt defervescence and the emergence of a blanching pink rash that starts on the trunk and spreads centrifugally while the child is now afebrile. That sequence is diagnostic and separates it from measles, where the rash appears at the fever peak after a prodrome, and from scarlet fever, where the rash is sandpapery with perioral pallor and a strawberry tongue. Roseola is a common cause of febrile convulsion during the fever phase, which is worth mentioning to parents who have witnessed one. No treatment or exclusion is required and the rash fades within a few days without desquamation.
key_points: Rash appearing as the fever breaks is the defining feature of roseola infantum.
The child is characteristically well once afebrile, which supports the diagnosis.
Measles rash appears during high fever after cough, coryza and conjunctivitis.
No investigation or antibiotic is required for a well child with a blanching exanthem.
Any non blanching element or ill appearance overrides the diagnosis and demands sepsis assessment.
explanation.pearls: Human herpesvirus 6 accounts for roughly a third of first febrile convulsions in children under two, so a brief convulsion during the fever phase of roseola does not itself indicate a more serious illness or warrant lumbar puncture in an otherwise well child over twelve months.

subtopic_detail: Refusal to use one arm in a toddler after being lifted by the hand, with no swelling and no bony tenderness
stem:
You are the emergency department resident seeing a two year old girl brought in by her father twenty minutes after he lifted her by the hand up a kerb as she stumbled. He and her older brother both saw it happen. She cried immediately and has not used the left arm since.

She is now settled on her father's lap, playing with a toy in her right hand, and holds the left arm slightly bent at the elbow with the palm turned down against her body. She has no other injuries and there are no concerns about her care at home.

data_table.Examination: Left arm held in slight flexion and pronation, no swelling, deformity or bruising anywhere on the limb, no tenderness over the clavicle, humerus, forearm or wrist, mild discomfort on attempted supination at the elbow, hand warm and pink with a normal radial pulse, moves fingers normally

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Perform a reduction manoeuvre at the elbow and observe her for return of normal use of the arm before discharge
options.rationale: A typical traction mechanism with the arm held pronated and no swelling, deformity or bony tenderness is a pulled elbow, and either supination with flexion or hyperpronation restores function within minutes. Reduction is both the treatment and the confirmation of the diagnosis. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Request radiographs of the elbow and forearm first and arrange reduction only once a fracture has been formally excluded
options.rationale: Radiographs are normal in a pulled elbow because the radial head subluxation reduces or is not visible, so they add radiation and delay without changing management. Imaging is indicated when the history is atypical, when there is swelling, deformity or focal bony tenderness, or when a reduction attempt fails. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Apply a broad arm sling for comfort and arrange review in the fracture clinic within forty eight hours for reassessment
options.rationale: Immobilising the arm leaves a readily treatable subluxation in place and condemns the child to two more days of not using the limb. A sling is appropriate for an undisplaced fracture awaiting review, not for a condition curable at the bedside in seconds. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Refer her to the orthopaedic registrar for assessment of the elbow and definitive management of the arm she is not using
options.rationale: Reduction of a pulled elbow is a core emergency department skill and specialist referral is an unnecessary escalation. Orthopaedic involvement is warranted only after two failed reduction attempts or where imaging shows a fracture. (Source: RCH CPG: Pulled elbow)

options.text: Undertake a skeletal survey and make a child protection notification before any attempt is made to treat the affected arm
options.rationale: A limb injury in a toddler always warrants a safeguarding thought, but here the mechanism is classical, independently witnessed, consistent with the findings and there are no other injuries or care concerns. An inconsistent or changing history, or bruising in unusual sites, would make this the priority. (Source: RCH CPG: Child abuse)

explanation.summary: Pulled elbow, or radial head subluxation, occurs when longitudinal traction on a young child's extended pronated arm allows the annular ligament to slip over the radial head and become trapped in the radiocapitellar joint. It peaks between one and four years because the radial head is not yet fully developed and the ligament is lax, and it becomes rare after five. The child characteristically refuses to use the arm and holds it pronated and slightly flexed, but is otherwise comfortable and shows no swelling, which is what separates it from a fracture. Both hyperpronation and supination with flexion are effective, with hyperpronation succeeding slightly more often and causing less distress, and a palpable click at the radial head predicts success. Recurrence happens in around a quarter of children, so parents should be advised to lift the child under the arms rather than by the hands.
key_points: The mechanism is axial traction on a pronated extended arm, often lifting a child by the hand.
Absence of swelling, deformity and bony tenderness is what permits reduction without imaging.
Hyperpronation or supination with flexion both reduce the subluxation within minutes.
Return of spontaneous use within about fifteen minutes confirms the diagnosis.
Image the elbow if the history is atypical, if there is focal tenderness or if two attempts fail.
explanation.pearls: If the child is not using the arm within fifteen to thirty minutes of a technically satisfactory reduction, obtain elbow radiographs rather than repeating the manoeuvre a third time, because an occult supracondylar or proximal radial fracture is then the more likely explanation.

sources.label: BMJ Best Practice: Radial head subluxation
